problem: Source lists St. John's nature as 'the rover, the aspirant, the poet, the priest'. 'Aspirant' means one who strives/aspires (his ambition, stressed again in 32.57); MODERN 'the dreamer' softens it into passivity and loses the ambition theme.
new_text: And then she would pout like a disappointed child; a wistful cloud would soften her radiant liveliness; she would snatch her hand from his and turn away in brief irritation from his look, at once so heroic and so martyrlike. St. John, no doubt, would have given the world to follow her, call her back, hold on to her when she left him like this; but he would not give one chance at heaven, nor surrender, for the paradise of her love, one hope of the true, eternal Paradise. Besides, he could not confine everything in his nature—the wanderer, the striver, the poet, the priest—within the limits of a single passion. He could not—he would not—trade his wild field of missionary work for the drawing rooms and the peace of Vale Hall. I learned this much from him directly, in an advance I once, despite his reserve, dared to make upon his confidence.

problem: Source: 'the eye is well managed: the colour, light, expression, are perfect.' MODERN 'the eye is perfectly done: ... are perfect' inflates the measured 'well managed' and, after this round's repair restored 'perfect', leaves an awkward doubled 'perfect'.
new_text: He continued to gaze at the picture: the longer he looked, the more firmly he held it, the more he seemed to want it. "It is like her!" he murmured; "the eye is well done: the color, light, expression are perfect. It smiles!"

problem: Source 'Won in youth to religion, she has cultivated my original qualities' means religion won him in youth. MODERN 'Won over to religion in my youth, she has cultivated...' makes the dangling participle attach to 'she' (religion), so it reads as though religion was won over; the referent of 'she' is unclear on first hearing.
new_text: "No. There is this difference between me and deist philosophers, who believe in God but not in revelation: I believe; and I believe the Gospel. You chose the wrong word. I am not a pagan but a Christian philosopher—a follower of the faith of Jesus. As His disciple I embrace His pure, merciful, generous teachings. I champion them: I am sworn to spread them. Religion won me in my youth, and she has cultivated my original qualities like this: from the tiny seed of natural affection, she has grown the towering tree of love for humanity. From the wild, stringy root of human integrity, she has raised a proper sense of divine justice. The ambition to win power and fame for my wretched self, she has transformed into the ambition to expand my Master's kingdom; to win victories for the banner of the cross. This is what religion has done for me; making the best use of the raw material; pruning and training nature. But she could not root out nature: nor will nature be rooted out until this mortal puts on immortality."

problem: Source contrasts the blessing of kin with 'the ponderous gift of gold: rich and welcome enough in its way, but sobering from its weight'. MODERN drops 'rich' ('welcome enough in its way'), losing the half of the concession that plays on the wealth theme.
new_text: I studied him. It seemed I had found a brother: one I could be proud of—one I could love; and two sisters, whose qualities were such that when I knew them only as strangers, they had inspired me with genuine affection and admiration. The two women on whom, kneeling on the wet ground and peering through the low, latticed window of Moor House kitchen, I had gazed with so bitter a mixture of fascination and despair—they were my close relatives; and the young, distinguished gentleman who had found me almost dying on his doorstep was my own blood relation. Glorious discovery for a lonely soul! This was wealth indeed!—wealth for the heart!—a mine of pure, warm affections. This was a blessing, bright, vivid, and exhilarating;—not like the heavy gift of gold: rich and welcome enough in its way, but sobering under its weight. I clapped my hands in sudden joy—my pulse leapt, my blood thrilled.
